analysis.one_liner: Strips the labor board of power to order employers to restore work they moved or outsourced.
analysis.headline: The Senate bill never got a vote: it was referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on September 8, 2011 and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the National Labor Relations Act to take away one of the National Labor Relations Board's remedies. The board could no longer order an employer to bring back work it had moved, subcontracted, or outsourced, and could not require an employer to invest in a particular plant. It would also apply retroactively to any case the board had not yet decided when the bill became law.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers — especially manufacturers considering relocating or outsourcing work — would gain protection from board orders that reverse those moves. The bill grew out of the widely reported dispute in which the NLRB filed a complaint against Boeing for placing a production line in South Carolina, a right-to-work state, after labor disputes at its Washington unionized plants; business groups argued the board was improperly dictating where companies may invest.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employers that relocate or outsource work

how_it_helps.text: The bill removes the board's power to order an employer to restore or reinstate any work, production line, or equipment that was moved, and to rescind relocations, transfers, subcontracting, or outsourcing decisions.

It also bars the board from requiring an employer to make any initial or additional investment at a particular plant, facility, or location, shielding business siting and investment decisions from board remedies.
The change would apply retroactively to any complaint not finally decided by the NLRB when the bill became law, wiping out pending cases of this kind.

analysis.who_pays: Workers who file unfair labor practice charges would lose the remedy of having work restored if the board finds their employer moved, outsourced, or relocated work to retaliate against union activity. The board's ability to deter retaliatory relocation would shrink accordingly.

drawbacks.text: The bill eliminates a specific remedy available to workers under the National Labor Relations Act: if the board finds an employer moved or outsourced work to punish union activity, it could no longer order that work restored or the relocation rescinded.
The retroactivity provision would apply the new limits to complaints already pending before the board, changing the rules mid-case for workers whose grievances were already filed.

Supporters' strongest argument for the bill — that the board should not dictate where a company builds a plant or invests — is a genuine concern about regulatory overreach into business decisions; the bill responds to that by removing the remedy entirely rather than narrowing it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill protects business siting and investment decisions from board orders, which supporters saw as government interference. The cost falls on workers: it removes the only remedy that can undo a retaliatory move of work, and applies the removal retroactively to pending cases. Whether that trade is worth it depends largely on how often relocations are actually retaliatory, which is exactly the dispute the board would no longer be allowed to resolve.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate labor committee, which never took it up, and it died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Senator Lindsey Graham introduced the bill on September 8, 2011, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
Nineteen Republican senators signed on as cosponsors; no Democrat did.
The bill received no further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — and expired with the 112th Congress.
Its House companion (H.R. 2587, the same-named bill) did pass the House in September 2011 along party lines, but the Senate never took up the measure.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers, including Boeing, came out ahead: the complaint the bill targeted was ultimately settled without the board ordering work returned, and this bill died without ever threatening pending NLRB remedies. Workers' existing remedies under the National Labor Relations Act were left intact by the bill's failure.

for.name: Lindsey Graham
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, which would bar the NLRB from ordering employers to restore relocated or outsourced work; his state was the site of the Boeing plant at the center of the NLRB dispute.

for.name: Business groups and employers
for.what_they_did: Publicly backed legislation to stop the NLRB's complaint against Boeing and curb board remedies against relocating or outsourcing employers; the House version passed in September 2011 amid this campaign.

against.name: Tom Harkin
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee never scheduled a hearing or vote on the bill, leaving it to die in committee.

against.name: Labor unions and worker advocates
against.what_they_did: Opposed efforts to strip the NLRB's remedy against retaliatory relocation during the Boeing dispute.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 cosponsors were Republicans and the sponsor was Republican; the bill sat in committee under Democratic leadership and no Democrat cosponsored it.

industries.industry: Manufacturers that relocate or outsource production (notably Boeing)
industries.note: The bill would shield employers from NLRB orders reversing relocations, transfers, or outsourcing, including the board's pending complaint over Boeing's South Carolina production line. That removes the main deterrent to moving work in retaliation for union activity, at workers' expense.

industries.industry: Labor unions and workers in NLRB proceedings
industries.note: Workers would lose the remedy of having work restored if the board finds a move or outsourcing was retaliatory, and the retroactivity clause would erase pending cases. Unions opposed this and similar bills during the Boeing fight.
